The appellants are the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and therefore a suit was for a mere declaration simpliciter could not lie. On appeal by the defendants, the Trial Court held that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court also held that since the plaintiff had not been in de facto possession no injunction could be granted and a suit to restrain defendant No 1 from interfering with his possession of property. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable; that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff having not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the said suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. There can, therefore be no doubt that after the Sixth Amendment became effective in regard to land used primarily for growing coconut trees and garden produce, the jurisdiction of Civil Court was ousted by virtue of section 58(2) from settling deciding or deal with any questions which is by or under the Act required to he settled, decide or dealt with. [1024C E] 2.1 The jurisdiction is, therefore vested in the Mamlatdar under Section 7 read with Section 58(1) and Section 58 (2). [1025E F] 3.2 In cases of threatened wrongful possession section 8A says that any tenant in possession shall be entitled to recover immediate possession of such land in the manner prescribed by or thereunder unless it is shown that his tenancy was terminated in the mode authorised by section 9. Even in cases of threatening wrongful possession Section 8A does not preclude the institution of a suit by a tenant for restoration of possession from a trespasser. If the defendant who is sued as a trespasser raises a plea of tenancy, a question arises whether his plea of ' tenancy can be decided by the Civil court as incidental to the grant of relief for possession or is the Civil Judge precluded from deciding the same in view of section 7 read Section 58 read with section 58 (1) of Act.

The petitioners are engaged in the construction industry. They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". The Corporation resisted the claim on the ground that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act and, therefore, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. A little more information about the purpose and object of the Corpora tion would be useful for proper understanding of the case. The Corporation was a company incorporated under the . The main object of this Corporation as seen from the Memorandum of Association is to preserve the traditional arts and crafts and also to popularise handicrafts and handloom items in the State of Himachal Pradesh and other parts of the country and abroad. In order to achieve this primary objec tive, the Corporation gives training to artisans, weavers and cracksmen in various traditional arts & crafts. During the period of training, the trainees are paid a stipend by the Corporati tion. Upto 31st March 1987, the Corporat ion has imparted training to as many as 1662 persons in different areas like carpet weaving, handloom, painting, metal crafts etc. Apart from giving training, they also ensures marketing support to the artisans and cra draftsmen by purchasing their products at remunerative prices and sell them through the marketing network of the Corporation. It is thus a service oriented organisation helping the village artisans & cragesmen to produce and market their products on remunerable prices. It was further stated that the village artists and cra Draftsftsmen made different items on a piece rate basis and in some cases, they execute the work in their own homes. The financial aspect of the corporation is stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it is disappointing. It has suffered huge loss and the total losses accumulated hitherto is Rs.69.77 lakhs. However, for the purpose of preserv ing and promoting traditional arts, the corporation has been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that since the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of tho State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. With these facts, the Court directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioners on par with his counterparts doing identical work under the same employer. In the immediate aftermath of the decision in Randhir Singh case there were bumper cases filed in this Court for enforcement of the right to equal pay for Equal work. The Court, therefore directed the Corporation to fix pay scale admissible to regular employees does not arises. A few more information regarding the purpose & object of Corpora tation has been keep alive. However to avoid and minimise further losses, it was stated that in service, merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or sheearns also by experience as much as by other means. Apartfrom that, the court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. The petitioners were claiming wages payable to the carpenters in Government service. The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical location though owned by tho same master. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the said master in the same establishment, the principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" cannot be enforced. This was also the view expressed in Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Anr., ; , at 245. In these circumstances, it may now turn to the principle upon which the petitioners ' case is rested.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, (exhibit A) in favour of her husband Sadagopalachar, died in December 1908. According to the plaint under the will respondent I was entitled only to a life interest in items 1 and 2 and that on her death the said items would vest in respondents 2 to 4 and respondent 5 respectively. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against respondent I in respect of items 3, 4 and 5 and a declaration that respondent I had only a life interests in items I and 2. The trial court held that the will was genuine and valid to the extent of the share belonging to the testatrix. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that at the relevant date Lakshmma had a subsisting interest in half the share even in the suit properties, items 1, 4, 5 and 6 were not entitled to any share in the said properties. The High Court also observed that even if it had found in favour Of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it was held that he had entirely failed to prove that the money for purchase of items I, and 2 came out of any bequest under Annaji 's will (ex exhibit A) or the incomes from the properties covered by the gift deed (ex Exhibit D). Held, that the High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the will and put her signature on it when she was in a sound disposing state of mind. The onus was heavy on him to remove any such legitimate doubts in the matter.

The appellants were selling Arcons known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" manufactured by the appellant company, which was used in the manufacture of Arcobons. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbons manufactured by it could be covered by the entry under consideration. It further held that the use which is generally made of the arc carbonons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The High Court also dismissed the appeal without taking further evidence. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the word "electrode" to describe them, suggesting a connection with electricity, nor their utilisation in a process involving application of electrical power could convert them into "electrical goods" as contemplated by the Entry in the Madras Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The term "accessories" is used in several entries such as entry No. 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, Entry No. 10 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and Entry No 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speakers. Our object in indicating the nature of entries, amdist which entry No 4 occurs, is to show that some precision has been attempted in making the entries. When it was intended to confine the entry to particular gadgets and "parts thereof" the entry said so. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for use for a particular kind of instrument of gadget only, the article manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of apparatus would not cease to be covered under the intended Entry simply because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [564B C] The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that "the main use of the are carboons under considerment" was duly established to be the purpose of production in the projectors or other cinematographic equipment.

The petitioners challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by Section 15 of the (67 of 1957), herein after referred to as the Act. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty was being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State, the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Govern ment had to be used only for minerals and not for other pur pose. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The levy in question is not unreasonably heavy and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner. [438C] 1.2 In the instant case, the impost is made under a law made by the Central Gov ernment on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 304(b) applied. It is not an imposition made by a law making it a part of a consolidated fund. The burden of establishing that the levy is unreasonably heavy, is on the petitioners. It was urged that in the other States the royalty is being levied at the rate of Re. 1 per metric tonne of Black Trap and Hard Murrum from Rs.4 to Rs.7. [414D E] 1:3 In the case of such people who are described in the Rules and who invariably belong to the weaker sections of society the concession is shown under rule 21, whereas the mining lease may be given to persons mentioned in Rule 9. Under Rule 18 of the Rules the period of lease in the case o f minor minerals can be for a much longer period, it can be upto 10 years in respect of minor minerals except in the cases of ordinary sand, Kankar Mur ram Gravel and in the ease of ordinary Sand, Kandas Murram and gravel a lease can be granted upto three years, and the area or land covered by a mining lease is governed by Rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec tares in the Case of other minerals.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the Sangunatha Ammal Community and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The appellant contended that the temple being rounded two thousand years ago, by the member of his Community and since thereafter the management was always vests in the Community of the Community and there was no person who other than his elected trustees had at all time the rights of management, and control and of the deity. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge but allowed the appeal and set aside that of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the succession is "regulated by usage" and therefore the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 1 of 1925; (ii) that in view of the provisions of the Act, the appellant is not a hereditary trustees within the contemplation of section. HELD: (1) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [445 B] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , followed. (2) It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, it is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. In Black 's Law Dictionary the word "Succession ' is defined as follows: "The revolution of title to property under the law of descent and distribution". [427 C] State Of Madras vs Rama, ; followed.

The deceased, Viswanatham Pillai was the village Munsif (Headman). On April 26, 1971 at about 10.00 P.M., he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15) at No. 9. The younger brother of the deceased Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 P.m. He saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1), and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3). He ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sitting and fell down on the northern side of a sluice of the north Boothagudi channel. When he went near him, he was already dead. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and Pandurangam was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries two of which he described as incised and four as punctured, two more as punctured and the remaining one as a vertical incised wound. These were on the left side of his back. injuries are very severe and according to the doctor death was due to shock and hemorrhage on account of the injuries. It is clear that whosoever had inflicted these injuries definitely had the intention to cause the death of the victim. In the first information report which PW 4 lodged at the Thana, which was very close to the place of occurrence, inter alia, stated thus: "4 L159SCI/76 710 On hearing a noise to the effect 'younger brother, Karunakaran is running after stabbing me with knife, 'catch him '. I stood up and saw Karunakaran son of Orathur Ayyathurai Padayachi running eastwards from the place where I lay and my elder brother chasing him from behind. I too came running. It will be seen that at the time of lodging of the first Information Report only the present accused was implicated. Even so, later on four eye witnesses were produced implicating not only the accused but also two other accused. The High Court after appreciating the entire evidence rejected the evidence of these eye witnesses, namely, PW 1, 2, 3 and 5 and described them as "a bunch of liars", "unashamed liars and perjurers". The High court further held that there had been a history of a bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first accused and his father on the one hand and the deceased Viswanatam on the other. This is, therefore, a case where conviction of the accused depends on the sole testimony of a single witness. If the witness is absolutely reliable there can be no infirmity in convicting the accused. In that case even corroboration may not be sought for. ordinarily in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution, it would have hestitated to go into the facts to reappreciate the evidence. It was, however, not possible to adopt that course in this case where the testimony of the sole witness has been rejected with reference to the first second accused who was on the same boat with the appellant. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1,2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the appellant 's father.

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. Amarchand died on July 7, 1949. Thereafter the partnership was carried on by Mangaldas and Hiralal up to November 30, 1949, and on December 1, 1949 Ramesh son of Amarchand who had by then qualified as a solicitor joined the firm as the third partner. After the death of Amar Chand the arrangement between the various partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of the work done up to the death Of Amarchand the real receipts were to be divided amongst the firms and the real proceeds were to divided amongst all the firms. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis, but for the five assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 the respondents claimed that they were not liable to income tax in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives of Amarachand after his death. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. For the assessment years 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34 could validly be served only for the assessment year 1950 51 and notices for the subsequent years were invalid. On appeal by the respondents the Tribunal held that even though for different reasons the amounts were not the income of the Hindu undivided family but merely represented inheritance or realisations or realisableisations of assets of Amar sons after his demise, they were liable to pay out of the estate of the deceased on those amounts to the extent of the Estate as the estate was liable for tax on the amounts received by the heirs, and legal representative just as the deceased Amarchand would have been had he not died. Held, that the fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24B and cannot be extended beyond that legitimate field field. In re Sreemati Usharani Shoudhurani, , referred to.

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They challenged the Act and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. Their case was that article 16(3) under which the Act or the Rules purport to be made has been misunderstood as conferring a power to make, a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. The petitioners contended that the word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12 and the second clause then specifies a prohibition against discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. Held, that section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957, in so far as it relates to Telengana (and we say nothing about the other parts) and Rule 3 of tho Rules under it are ultra vires. The word ' State ' here was to be construed in the limited use given by the inclusive definition of residence within the State or Union territory prior to employment or appointment to an office is guaranteed. By the second cl, there can be no discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. Realising, however, that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States may have had to be prevented and a residential qualification may, therefore, have to he prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them he was charged with offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him in each of the three appeals for offences tinder section 52. On appeal by the State it was contended that the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the prosecution had failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees. It was probably for this reason that the definition clearly lays down that until an article despatched by post is delivered or can be said to be delivered that it will be deemed to be In course of trans portation by post from the time of its being delivered to a Post Office to the time when its being actually delivered to the sender or otherwise disposed of under Chapter VII. The object of the provision was to prevent postal articles 'in course of the transmission by post 'from being tampered with, and so the secreting, destruction etc., of postal article would frustrate or tend to frustrate their delivery to the addressees.

The appellants were charged with contempt of court. The complaint was adjourned to December 25, 1963. On October 11, 1963, the Nyaya Panchayat met and proceeded to hear the case. The order sheet stated that "Put up today the 25th December, 1963". The complainant and the accused were present. The statements of the complainant and his witnesses were recorded on oath. Bunna Prasad, in his affidavit stated that as the paper of the application was not properly stamped, he had no knowledge of the High Court 's stay order. He further added that "the Nyaya Panchayat was not satisfied for want of evidence by way of proper affidavit etc. , the Nyaya Panchayats proceeded with the case". The High Court held that the Nyaya Panchas were not well versed in law and procedure and the records maintained by them should not be judged in the same manner as that of ordinary courts. With respect, the High court held that it was the Sarpanch who had initially declared that the affidavit of the applicant was not proper and that the matter should file a proper affidavit in support of his allegations though the Sarpanch had admitted in his deposition that he had to authority to tell Mahabir that his affidavit was not correct. The High ' Court also rejected the explanation of the Panchas given before it because no mention of these was made in the order sheet dated December 25. 1963. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) It is not proved on the evidence that any such application was made before the Nyaya panchayat. No application dated December 21, 1963 which was not accepted by the Nyaya Gram Panchayat had been produced.

The appellant was charged with murder of a person who was sleeping in his cattle shed in village Bhadurpur Ghar, with a sword at about mid night on the night between June 14 15, 1960. The prosecution case was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and asked him to go to the Police Station, Ekdil, nine miles away and lodged a report. He delivered the sword which had been found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood. The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of investigation was sent up for trial, The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge believed Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant 's confessing to him that he did commit the murder of Sheo Swarup Sahai and that he deposited it stained with his human blood at the Police station on the day of the murder. The High Court, however, did not rely on this extra judicial confession. It relied on certain statements made by the appellant in his report dictated at the police Station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appel lant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish conclusively that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai, and that there were good reasons for Ujagar Singh not leaving his field whose crops he was watching against the neel gais. HELD: (i) The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person whom who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed. [206 E] (ii) It may be that having blurted out the truth to be proceeded to the police station and report the matter there, there is no reason for a person 's acting in a certain manner. It may also be that taking blurtling out the falsehood to Ujagar Singh, when taken by surprise, the appell lant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the nal police station, and report about it.

The appellants challenged the validity of the electoral roll, the calendar of events and the declaration of results of election. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of that notice, when sub rule (3) of Rule 4 prescribed that such claims and objection could be preferred only 30 days from that date. The appellants challenged this order by special leave to appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in doing so since if it agreed with the High Court on the question, it would become unnecessary to go into the other questions raised before us. [496C] 1.2 In the course of the discussion with the press reporters on that day, the Minister had stated that he had directed the Commissioner, Raipur Division, Raipur, that the date for inclusion of names in the electoral Roll could be extended if the election date was not affected. There was a further reference to dates of election to Bilaspur Municipal Committee having been adjourned twice before. It is difficult to place any reliance on the news item for the purpose of concluding that the Collector, Raipur had been informed about the defect and that the writ petition itself was presented on December 28, 1978. No satisfactory reason for the delay was set out in the petition.

The respondent company and its directors were prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) of the Companies Act, 1913 for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of that Act. The High Court acquitted the directors holding that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body meeting nor could it be so laid, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general Body meeting and lay the balance sheets and profit & loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act 1913 or section 220 of the . In appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balancesheet and profit account is a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. If no such balance sheet is laid before the general body, there could be no objection to that balance sheets not being utilised nor of compliance with the provisions contained in any of the four preceding sub sections. [416 A] (2) The finding of the High Court that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meeting. [417 B C] (3) Under section 134 the laying of a balance sheet or profit and losses account before the company in the general meeting is made obligatory. Under section 133 the failure to comply with section 131 is made punishable. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit loss account or the income and expenditure account as the case may be, have been laid before it at a general Meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to do so is made penal by the Act. [414 C] Gibson vs Barlon, ; , followed. (4) The liability of sending three copies of the Balance sheet and profits and loss accounts which are laid before such general body may have been forwarded under sub section (1), of section 132 cannot be complied with. While the appeal to a question of principle might be attractive, it cannot ignore the clear words of the section. Where the words of a section are very clear it is unnecessary to consider whether it embodies any principle and whether that principle is consistent with the principle as embodied a certain other sections which are differently worded. In interpreting a penal provision it is not permissible to give an extended meaning to the plain words of that section on the ground that a principle recognised in respect of certain other provisions Of law requires that this section should be interpreted is the same way. [413 D E] (5) The court there observed that the decision in Park vs Lawton, ; and Park vs lawton, , referred to.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal by a notification dated 26th January 1950. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The High Court quashed the conviction. Held, that section 5(1) Of the WestBengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949 was valid as it did not by itself make any distinction between cases and offences triable by the special court and those for the purpose of being tried by a Special Court. The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and was not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of cases".

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. By letter dated April 6, 1965 the Delhi Administration informed the Principal, Maulana Gandhi Medical College that the Vice Chancellor of the Delhi University in exercise of his emergency powers had granted him recognition as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students for the D.M.R.T. and M.B.S. courses of studies. The appellant was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview on August 7, 1972 for the post of Professor of radiotherapy but since the post was falling vacant in 1973 he did not appear for the interview. The Government of India Ministry of Health and Family Planning Department of Health by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the Delhi Adminis tration that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital. The Ministry of Finance by its Letter dated January 17, 1976 however informed the Secretary (Medical), Delhi Administration that it had no objection to designating him as Associate Professor and that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the post. In response to an advertisement of the Union Public Service Commission for the non teaching post of Radiologist, the appellant was asked by the Government to give up all connections with the Central Health Service. The letter further stated that the Government had no objections to designing him as a Associate Professor or Radiology (ex officio) in the Maulana New Azad Medical 25 College provided it was neither detrimental to his normal duties as a Radiologist nor any financial implications were involved. The respondent State of Punjab by its order dated January 9, 1979 informed the appellant that the post had fallen vacant in 1974 and that consequent upon the appointment of the appellant in Category `C ' of the Central health Service, the Administration had no objec tions to designate him as Assistant Professor. The order was challenged before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition holding that since the appellant had the essential qualification prescribed for teaching post the teaching experience gained by him while holding the post he held the post in the senior scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that speciality and 20% of the vacancies thereof were to be filled by direct recruitment in the manner specified in the Second Schedule, he was clearly eligible for appointment as Professor or radiology in the Medical College. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The post of Assistant Professor of Pathology (Ex officio) is a post belonging to Specialist Grade I which is equivalent to Supertime Grade II carrying a pay scale of Rs. 8(3) provides that 50% of vacancies in super time grade II to be filling in by promotion of General Duty Officers Grade I and Specialists Grade II officers in the ratio of 2 :3 and the remaining 50% Of the vacancies to be carried filled by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the posts in the junior scale who have rendered not more than six year ' teaching experience out of 12 years ' standing in the grade through the Union Government Public Service Commis sion. [27A B] 2. The qualifications and experience prescribed in Annexure I to the Second schedule determine the question of his eligibility for such promotion or appointment.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The dispute related to fixation of wages including minimum wages and this was covered by items Nos. 1, 3, 4, 22 and 26 in the Schedule attached to the order of reference. The Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items. The special leave in this Court was sought and granted in respect of two matters covering some of these items. In the course of arguments before this Court it was contended that (1) the Tribunal committed an error in fixing the minimum wage in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wages prevailing in other industries in that region, and (2) the principle laid down by this Court in French Motor Car Co. vs Its Workmen ; , followed. Held: (i) The Tribunal committed no error in arriving at this decision and consequently the total minimum wage fixed by it must also be deemed to have the same break up. As a result of the award, the Tribunal was entitled to fix the minimum wages in the company on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of the parties and in holding that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which is the average Minimum wage payable by those industries (1 ) [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 673, followed. (ii) The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed as that year was still running when the award was given by the Tribunal on the 11th January, 1964.

The assessee firm was a partnership firm. For the assessment year 1960 61, relevant to the accounting year 1959 60, after the assessee submitted its income tax return, it was asked by the Income Tax Officer during the income tax assessment proceedings to produce before him its books of account and other relevant papers. The assessee also produced before him a statement showing various creditors from whom it had borrowed on Hundis during the accounting years in question. In that statement it gave the lull names and address of the alleged creditors. After enquiry, the Income tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. The material portion of that notice reads as follows " Notice under section 147(2) of the Income ' tax Act 1961. Income Tax officer, Muzaffarpur Dated, the 3 6 1966. TO M/s Chugamal Rajpal, Muzaffar Nagar. Whereas (1) have reason to believe that your income chargeable the income of 1960 1961 in respect of which you are assessable to tax for the assessment years 19 19 19 has escaped assessment within the 444 meaning of section 147 of the Act, I therefore propose to re assess the income for the said assessment year and I hereby require you to deliver to me within 30 days from the date of service of this notice a return in the prescribed form of your income. The Income tax officer did not set out any reason for coming to the conclusion that this was a fit case for the issue of a notice under s 148. The Commissioner, however, issued a notice on the assessee under section 151(2). The assessee challenged the validity of that order as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notification on various grounds. As the assessee contended that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151 (2) and that the notice was valid because it did comply with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : The Commissioner had mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that this is a fit one for the issuance of a show cause notice under Section 148. [466C] (a) It is clear from the report submitted by the Incometax Officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner was produced. The order sheet recording the reasons of the income Tax Officer as required by section 148(2), was not produced. [427E F] (b) The Commissioner has mechanically accorded the permission.

The appellant was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of textiles. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the business which had been subjected to tax under the Act of 1918 had ceased at any time before 1948 or (b) whether there was a succession by another person for the person who was carrying On April 1, 1939, and therefore, the partnership business continued in the hands of the same person who had paid tax under section 25(4). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner also held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 26 (2) of the Income tax Act. The Tribunal however held that on May 30, 1939 there was discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 25 (3) and that the partnership in question had been discontinued in October/November 1937 or on May 31, 1939 and it was not in existence in 1948 so as to permit a succession to it taking place under the instrument of February 7, 1948. The High Court held that there was no succession within the mischief of section 26(2) and therefore the partnership firm could be said to have ceased at the date of the partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under s.25 (4). Held, that the question whether there has been a succession within section 26 or for the purpose of section 24 (4) was one of fact and not of law and must be decided on its own facts. The business which was taxed under the Income Tax Act of 1922 had ceased to exist before the benefit of section25 (3). The business in question was carried on by a person different from those who carried it on as a whole. The partnership was brought about by the instrument Of December 6, 1918 for the partners in the two firms were not the same. There was no cessation of business in so far as the original business of piece goods, yarn and banking was concerned. That business continued even in the possession of the firm after the partition of the partnership. The firm had been dissolved in October, 1943 or on June 30, 1940, and it could not be said that the same business on which tax had been charged under the 1922 Act of 1947 had ceased. Held, further, that there could be no question of the succession to the business carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 in so as the partnership was concerned because the firm was dissolved and it had been continued by two independent firms for the document of October 30, 1943, which was a complete change of ownership of all the businesses was necessary for purposes of section 23(2), before it could be held that it was the business of the partners that was carried in by the firm as a result of a transfer by an instrument executed on February 7. The fact that he was not taken on in the original partnership business also shows that the original firm business in respect of which alone the benefit had been claimed by one of the members of the erstwhile family and not by the whole family, though I express no opinion upon it, but even so that would be a case of succession rather than of discontinuance. The mere fact that the assessee was not taking on in April 1 1939, did not make any difference because the original assessment year was not a dissolution of the original one of 1947 and 1948.

The appellant 's suit based as it was on the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, was essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary property. Two things became necessary to determine for the purpose of giving relief to the plaintiff. One, her share in her husband 's share and two, her husband, 's own share in a coparcenary property, were thus clears : One, that in a partition between Khandappa and his two sons, there would be four sharers in the joint family properties, the fourth being Khandappa 's wife, the plaintiff 's son, and their two children each having a 1/4th share therein. Adding 1/3rd and 1/24th, the appellant claims a 7/24 th share in one of the joint families. The other three getting 1/2 share each would devolve upon his death on six sharers, the other being Khandappappa ' 's 1/6th share would devolve on his death. On the question whether the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th share by ignoring the 1/5th share which she would have obtained had there been a partition during her husband life time between him and his sons. HELD : (1) The view taken by the Bombay High Court in Rangubai Lalji vs Laxman Lalji, [1959] Stipp. 1 S.C.R. 394, that Explanation 1 to section 6 does not apply, that the proviso to that section is attracted and that the decision of the appeal must turn on the meaning to be given to Explanation 1 of section6. The interpretation which will further the intention of the legislature and remedy the injustice from which the Hindu women have suffered over the years, is truly to permit one 's imagination to boggle under the oppression of the reality that there was in fact no partition between the plaintiff and his coparceners immediately before his death, and that assumption, having been made once for the purposes of ascertaining the share of the deceased in the coparcener property, one cannot go back on that assumption and ascertain the share Of the heirs without reference to it. [765 E F] (2) The plain meaning of Explanation 1 is the subject matter of acute controversy between the parties. The plaintiff ' s suit based on the provision of section 30 of the Act was essentially one claim to recover a share from the defendant. The proviso to section six comes into play and the normal rule is excluded. [766 G] (3) The interpretation that Explanation I has to be read as enabling a person who has separated himself from the coparcenary before the death of the person in whose property the heirs claim a share. The fiction created by Explanation 1 has to he given its due and full effect as the fiction created under section 18A(9)(b). [767 A] (4) The assumption that Explanation1 has to have been given its true effect is not a processual step devised merely for the limited purpose of working out some other conclusion. It has to, be treated and accepted as a concrete reality, something that cannot be recalled just as a share allotted to a coparcener in an actual partition cannot generally be recalled.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were made by the Central Government under section 11(2) of the , providing for the vesting of the management of the life insurance business (which was called the controlled business) in India. The said regulations were amended on 21st January, 1977 and it provided that an employee belonging to Class I or class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on or after 1st September 1956 would retire on completion of 58 years of age but the appointing authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of the Corpora tion to do so, direct such employee to retire on 31st September, 1956. The amendment was made by a new sub regulation which was notified on September 3, 1966. The first proviso to section 11 provided that notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1) of section 11 or in any contract of service, the Central Govern ment might for the purposes of rationalising the pay scales of employees of insurers whose controlled business had been transferred to and vested in it or for the pur pose of reducing the remu neration payable to those employees in cases where in the interests of the corporation and its policyholders a reduction in the remuneration payable, or a revision of the other terms and conditions of service applicable, to employees or any class of them is called for, the central Government may, notwith standing anything contained In sub section 2(a) or in the , or in in any other law for the time being in force, alter (whether by way of reduction or otherwise) the remuneration and other terms of service to such extent and in such manner as it thinks fit, and if the alteration is not acceptable to any employee the Corporation may terminate his employ ment by giving him compensation equivalent to three months ' remuneration unless the contract of serv ice with such employee provided for a shorter notice of termination. The second proviso was added to section 49(2). The first sub clause was substituted by a fresh sub regulation whereby it was provided that where the Central Govt is satisfied that for the purpose of securing uniformity in the scales of pay of employees, whose controlled policy had been trans ferred to and vest in it, it is necessary so to do, or that in the public interest, the Corporation and its Policyholders a reduced wage structure may be fixed. The third proviso was substituted with effect from 20th June, 1979. The new sub clause provided that if an employee of Class I and class II officers appointed to Class III and Class IV and Class II who were appointed to that service on or before 1st Septem ber 1956, would on and from the appointed day become an employee Of the Corporation, and would hold his office therein by the same tenure, at the same remuneration and upon the same terms and condi tions and with the same rights and privileges as to pension and gratuity and other matters as he would have held the same on the appointed date if this Act had not been passed, and shall continue to do such things unless and until his employment in the Corporation was terminated and until His remuneration, terms and con cerned by the Corporatio n may be altered by the corporation. The proviso further provided that nothing contained in this sub section shall apply to any such employee who has, by notice in writing given to the Central government prior to the ap pointed day, intimated his intention of not becoming an employee. The appellants wrote a letter to the President with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial als of a Judge. The letter was addressed to the Governor of Punjab and Haryana High Court, the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Prime Minister. In that letter they said that Justice D.S. Tewatia of the Punjab and Punjab High Court visited the session division of Bhiwani and inspected the Courts from 14 February 1975 to 19 February 1975. In the letter they stated that the library of this Bar seems to be very poor. Then the Honourable Judge turned down the request and replied that it is never possible in the present practice of Government of India. If you want this kind of help then you should prepare yourself for the commu nist Government in India by creating such atmosphere in the country. At another stage also during the course of his discussion with the members of the Bar, the Judges of the High Court felt that the prevailing system of Government is not good in this country and therefore it must adopt the communist form of Govern ment which can save the nation. The appellants took a copy of their letter to Chief Justice of Punjab & Haryana High court, the chief Minister of State and the Chief Jus tice of Punjab. The Chief Justice told them that the closed cover could reach the Honble Chief Justice, A notice was issued by the High court on 12 March 1975 as follows: "Letter dated 20th February, 1975 a copy by Shri Virender Kumar, Advocate, Advocate General of Haryana, quite fairly stated that in view of this Hon ' Supreme Court the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of Court, one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. Therefore, the deponent tenders his apology to this Honble Court, for the same and prays for its acceptance." The Full Bench of the high Court consisting of Justice Surjit Singh Sandhawalia, Justice Prem Chand Jain and Jus t ice Bhupinder Singh Dhillon extracted portions from the affidavit of the appellants to which references have been made. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri. Each of the appel lants affirmed an affidavit in this pattern. It was necessary to state here that if any Judge address es on political problems or controversies the Judge exposes himself to discussion by public. The deponent tendered his apology for the said purpose and prayed for its con tention. The Full Court also did not mention which particular portion of the letter constituted contempt of court. It is necessary to further state here, that if on facts it appears that the Judge did say things or matters about politics such utterances or views or observations will be the personal opinions expressed by the Judge, and, therefore, the protec tive umbrella of the Court cannot be used by way of bringing the critics on the charge of contempt of courts. The judgment is set aside.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. Suraj Mall Mohta was also the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. A reference had been made by the Central Government under section 5(1) of the Act before 58 450 1st September, 1948, of the case of the petitioner along with the cases of Suraj Mall Keta and other members of his family may be referred to the Commission for investigation. On the 15th of September, 1953, a report to this effect was made by it to the Central Govern ment under section 6(1), requesting that the case be investigated and they were called upon to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure "B" of the petition, to the petitioner. On 12th April 1954, the Commission notified the petitioners that their cases had been referred for investigation and they should furnish certain materials as detailed therein. The present petition under article 32 of the Constitution was filed for the issue of appropriate writs restraining the Commission from taking any action against the petitioner under the provisions of the , on the ground that the provisions Of sections 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Indian Income tax Act had become void being discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the constitution of India. Held, that section 5 (1) Of the Indian Incometax Act and sub section (4) of section 5 of the impugned Act deal with all persons who have similar characteristics and similar properties, the common characteristics being that they are persons who had not truly disclosed their income and have evaded payment of taxation on income. It is not possible to hold that all such persons who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 of the Income tax ' Act and come under it, but without in any way deciding or even expressing any opinion on that question, they cannot be dealt with under the provi sions of section 4 Of the impugned act. The procedure thus prescribed by the impugned provisions is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure prescribed under the Act.

The respondent, a company registered under section 26 of the Indian Companies Act 1913, was carrying on business in matters of inland and foreign trade. The primary objects of the Federation as given in the Memorandum of Association are "regulation of hours of work, payment of wages, leave, holiday terms of service and other conditions of work of persons employed in shop commercial establishment, establishments for public entertainment or amusement and other establishments and to provide for certain matters connected therewith". Section 1(4) indicates its extent and application. It shall apply in the first instance only to the municipal areas, notified areas of Delhi and New Delhi etc., but Government may by notification extend or apply it to shops and establishments in the other local area or areas. The definitions of " commercial establishment" and "shop" given in sub sections (5), (9) and (27) of section 2 are material for our purpose. They read " Commercial Establishment" means any premises wherein any trade, business or profession is carried on, or (b) any work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary thereto is carried On and includes a society registered under the , and charitable or other trust, whether registered or not which carries on any business, trade or profession. " Establishment" mean any premises where goods are sold, either by retail or wholesale Or where services are rendered to customers, and includes an office, a stoic room, godown, warehouse or work place, whether in the same premises or otherwise used in connection therewith or in connection With such trade or business but does not include a shop or a factory registered under tho , or theaters, cinemas, restaurants eating houses, residential hotels, clubs or other places of public amusement or entertainment. " establishment" means a shop, a commercial establishment and a residential hotel, restaurant, eating house, theatre or other place of public entertainment to which this Act applies and includes such other establishment as Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be an establishment for the purposes of the Act. " Commercial establishment" is defined in section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The main object of the said Act as stated in its preamble is "regulation for hours of business, payment, of wages etc., of persons engaged in shop, commercial establishments, establishments, for public institution or amusement or other establishments". Section 2(7) defines 'establishment ' to mean any building where goods were sold, whether by retail, wholesale or where services were rendered to customer. The definition of "commercial establishment" includes a shop and a commercial Establishment. The term "shops" is wide enough to include the idea of profit, yet the definition of the mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question whether they carry on a trade, how can it be denied that the Council carry on business. They are incorporated; they have a secretary and they print books, they sell those books, them do all that is ordinarily done in carrying on the business of a bookseller. The mere fact of the matter is that the respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen. As regards the preliminary objection, it was held by this Court that the activity of the Association amounts to "work in connection" with, inter alia, of "industry" as defined in s.2(j) of ' the Act, which in consequence had no application. From the side of the present appellant, at first a half hearted attempt was made to show that the Federation is carrying on a profession as it is "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". This contention was negatived by this court in Management of the Union of the India Chamber of Commerce and Industry vs Their workmen, Shri R. K. Mittal, [1971] 1 S.C.R. No. 869.

The respondent was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of certain land known as Ausanganj State in Benaras. The district of Benaras was formerly part of Oudh territory. By a Treaty between the East India Company Nawab Asfuddaula in or about the year 1775, the province of Benares was ceded to the British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhithala untoly in perpetuity to Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the Jagir and became entitled to merely a pension. The letter by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8/ was dated July 1837 and from H. Elliot Esqr., the Secretary Sadar Board of Revenue N.W.P. Allahabad, to J. Thompson Esqrs., Offg. Secretary to Lt. Government, N. W.P., Allahabad, who held that the amount which had been received by the successors of Babu Harnarain Singh varied from year to year and was not agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income. Held, that the allowance was revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income under section 4 (3)(ixviii) Of the Income Tax Act. Maharajkumar Gopal Saran Narain Singh vs Commissioner of Income tax Bihar and Orissa, ; , followed.
