The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation and some other private operators filed writ petitions in the High Court. The writ petitions were rejected by the High court on the ground that the preference contemplated by the proviso to section 63(7) contemplated exclusion of the 'non preferred ' class if sufficient number of applicants from the preferred classes were available. The decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case was distinguished on the grounds that in that case the court interpreted the word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) in the back ground of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A of the Act, under the former of which the State Transport Undertaking would have preference whereas under the latter the State transport Undertaking would had a monopoly. The Karnataka State Transport Appellate Tribunal set aside the grant of three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corpora tion and instead granted three permits to private operators and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development corporation from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the Proviso to section 64(7), the applications from the ' non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the application, which was upheld by this Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Karnataka that the State Road transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Courts were wrong in distinguishing the decision of the Supreme Court in that fashion. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50, and for 194950. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 6 63 denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under sections 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act, and that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title, Purushottam Raju. This appeal is brought by special leave. HELD: The word 'assessment ' used in section 19(l)(c), does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule is beyond the rule made power of State Government either under section 19 (1) or section 19 or section19(2) (c) or of the Central Act. [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, , Chatturam vs C I.T. Bihar, ; Chattaram vs C .I. T. Bihar; , Chattyuram vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, ; and Chattramuram vsC.I., Bihar; referred to.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Government of Saurashtra. He filed a written statement on September 4, 1954 and an enquiry was held by him. The Enquiry Officer made a report and on or about January 7, 1955, the following notice was issued to him calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from serv ice "To Shri Bhaishanker A. Joshi, Accountant, Rajkot Central Prison (Under suspension) Charges framed against you under this office. No. C/ 14 dated 27 3 54 and in particular the charges of having accepted illegal gratification from prisoner Ratilal Jivan have been established to the satisfaction of Government. You are hereby asked to showcause why the punishment of dismissal from service should not he inflicted upon you. " The plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal, dated February 2/4, 1955 was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal succeeded before the District Judge, Central Saurashtra, inasmuch as he declared the order dated February 3/4 1955, illegal and inoperative. The High Court held that there had been a breach of article 31(2), as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against the plaintiff. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court erred in holding that there was a breach on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy and of the Enquiry Officer. The State of West Bengal vs Abdul Majid, [1958] S.C.R. 811, referred to.

The appellant was granted a lease of the coal and coal mining rights in respect of 400 bighas out of his total area. The lease deed provided that the northern boundary of the leasehold land was to be drawn between the two leaseholds. The western boundary was shown as the northern boundaries of the lease hold of Samanta. On June 15,1900, the appellant made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The Commissioner appointed by the Court tested the position of the six trijunction pillars shown in the map of lease dated November 23, 1900, and found that two of the trijram pillars were in their correct positions. On these allegations the appellant asked for the following reliefs: (a) That the intermediate boundary line between the appellants ' coal land and the defendants ' coal mining right be ascertained and fixed; (b)That a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the plaintiffs ' coal mines and removing coal therefrom. The respondents denied that they had encroached on the plaintiff ' coal lands and stated that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court held that the defendant had encroached Upon the appellant 's coal land, that the lease deed was not a valid document and that the boundary could more satisfactorily be fixed with reference to the plans annexed to the subsequent lease deeds executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents. On appeal the High Court accepted all the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The finding of the courts below that the disputed extent of land was part of the holding of the respondents, is vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. (ii) The onus was upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove that the knowledge of his father wag within three years of the suit and that is all. If he proves this, then to succeed in the plea of limitation the defendant has to prove satisfactorily that the fact that the property was in his possession became known to the plaintiff more than three years prior to the suit. (iii) The burden of proving that the title was in the possession of the defendant within three year of the date of filing of the suits, and that was all. , therefore, on the respondents it could not be held that they were guilty of any breach of contract.

The appellant, a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It is said that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the Tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal also pointed Out that no effort was made by it to prove which had actually happen. It also held that there was nothing for it to justify before the Industrial Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A). [826 C] (ii) The employer could defend the actions under r . 18(b) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there were in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power conferred. But the Tribunal has pointed out, that the employer did not attempt to do so before it. It satisfied itself by producing two witnesses but withholding the important witness on this question. [826 D] (iii) The industrial court in its opinion had the right of inquiring into the cause that might had led to the termination of services even under r, 18(c). But the tribunal has pointed Out, that it did not accept the evidence of the two witnesses who were produced, it cannot be said to have gone wrong. [827 E] (iv) The appellant failed to satisfy the Tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of power in this case was bona bonafide and was therefore not colourable. It could have easily done so by producing satisfactory evidence; but it seems to have rested upon its right that no such justification was required and, therefore, having failed to justify its action must suffer the consequences.

The appellants were the owners of a cinema theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Geneva, right to exhibit cinematograph films was granted to the latter on certain conditions. "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 in the Court of Small Causes Ahmedabad against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated October 27,1954 to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By order dated December 1, 1960, the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and Cododod were bound and liable to allow Filmistan to exercise its "exhibition rights" in the cinema theatre; that Raval, and Fraqui, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibits any picture in contravention of the terms and condi tions of the agreement. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and restored that of the Trial Court. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants: (1) that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to 'be put to the witnesses for Filmistans, and (2) that in any event the case or any part thereof was not likely to be disposed of on these issues. HELD : (i) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. 442 This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869 that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Code to the entire proceedings in a civil court. To interpret the expression 'case ' as an entire proceeding only and not a part of the proceeding imposes an unwarranted restriction on the exercise of powers of superintendence and may result in certain cases in denying relief to the aggrieved litigant where it is most needed and may results in the perpetration of gross injustice. But it was not decided in Major s. Khanna vs Col. Brig. C. J Dillan, [1893] 1 K.B.D. 891, followed. (ii) The consent decree must be held to create a bar of res judicata as far as the question of document of November 27 is concerned. [436 E F] (iii) The Court gave no finding expressly or by implication on the issue of resjudicata or any other issue.

The respondent, a pilot Officer was granted a permanent commission in the Indian Air Force and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. Under that scheme the ex military official were appointed on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. Pursuant to the said scheme the respondent was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State of U.P. The terms and conditions contained in the said order included the above term relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms and condi tion he was appointed to the post till 30th August, 1985 and it was again extended upto 31st March, 1983 by an order dated 1st June, 1983. Again the term was extended upto 30th of August,1985 by an Order dated 1 6 1983. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms & conditions contained therein includ ing the above terms relating to period of appoint ment and on accepting the term and conditions he was appoint ed as Secretary. The order was to be effective from the date of receipt of termination order and no charges were men tioned therein against the 1st respondent. The Respondent aggrieved by the said orders filed a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was entitled to salary upto the period he was enti tled to remain in service, i.e., 30th September, 1985 unless there was a further extension. But on 29.3.1985 the service of the 1 st respondent was terminated by the issue of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to be allowed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the interim order entitled him to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period beyond 30th 885 of August 1985. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24.3 1988 directed that the respondent be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. Even the order passed on Review on 26.7.1988 does not make out that the Respondent had put forward at that stage such a case.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The prosecution case was that the accused had no motive to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. The Sessions Judge held that the prosecution had failed to establish any motive and that the evidence of the witnesses was 'discrepant, conflicting and improbable. He thought that the defence had made an attempt to improve its case which was originally based on circumstantial evidence to make it appear as if P.W. 3 had also seen the stabbing. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. An order of acquittal can be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial", and compelling reason". [368C] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , referred to. 2. The principles are now well settled. At one time it was thou ht that an order of acquitting could be setaside for " substantial and compelling grounds" only, and Courts use to launch upon a searchto discover those 'substantial and enabling reasons". However, the 'formula ' of "substantial" and " compelling reasons", "good and sufficiently cogent reasons" and 'strong reasons" are now firmly settled. [368E F] San watwat Singh vs State Of Rajasthan, A.I.R.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was convicted for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal and convicted him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the President is given the power to appoint the Judges of the High Court as well as of the Chief Justice of the high Court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief justice of India, the Governor of the State and in a case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Jus tice, the Chief Judge of a High Court can be removed from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; (ii) the power under clause (c) is the President and it is in this manner that section 6(1) (c), which specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 161(or section 165 of the Indian Penal Code, or under sub section (2) or sub section 3A) of section 5 of this Act, alleged to have been committed by a public servant, except with the previous sanction, (a) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his Office; and (b) in case of a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his offices save by or with the sanction of the Central Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to punish a High court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution. [835C] 2.1 In the case, the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of theHigh Court from his place in order to enable that authority to grant sanction for prosecution of the Judge under the provisions of section 6 of the Act and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which such an opinion can be formed and there is no vertical superior with legal authority enabling obtaining of information from the concerned Judge. [889E] 2:2 The President, therefore, being the authority Competent to appoint and to remove Judge, of course in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article 124, clauses (4) & (5), placed before the President, a Judge by warrant, under his hands and seal, after consultationwith such of the Judges. [879E F] 2 :3 The power of appointment and removal of a judge other than those of the highest Court is not contemplated by section 6, but only for the purpose of deciding whether the offence under clause(e) of possession of disproportionate assets which the Public servant cannot satisfactorily account is made out prima facie. [869C] 4:1. The President has no power or authority to remove any Judge either from his residence or from his post except with a previous sanction.

The respondent was a member of a Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were the members of a scheduled caste. Abhaoy P.ada Saha, a member belonging to the Sunri caste which was a Scheduled Castes belonged. Abdhoy, Pada, described himself in the nomination paper as "a member of the Sunari caste which is a Scheduled caste". Abhiman Pada was a Member of a Schedule Caste. An objection to this nomination contending that Abhutoy Pa was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Caste group because he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant was a " Sunri" by caste and had not been proved to belong to the Scheduled Castes specified in item 40. [390 E] (2) The expression "excluding Saha" meant excluding a smaller Caste group called Sahas, must, without more, refer to a caste group within the Suniti caste. It is legitimate to think that when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste, the other must be a caste. [391 E] In the instant case, the Tribunal came to its conclusion that it had not taken any steps in this case and the appellant was thereby excluded from his membership. [392 G] (3) The finding that Sahas formed a distinct caste wholly outside the Suni caste and they had been specifically excluded in item40 for greater safety o prevent them from claiming to be Sunris by reason of their origin, could not alter the natural interpretation of the words in the order.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It is said that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the police on 1 12 1948, and in conjunction with the latter, a trap was laid for the appellant. The complainant and the Sub Inspec tor were then taken to the appellant 's residence on 4 12 1948 and in connection with the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement was tween the complainant and his wife and the appellant, an application form for permission to occupy the building as caretaker. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a pugree of Rs 29,500 and he was further charged under s 19(2) of that Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caRetaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view of his intended departure. The prosecution case was that the accused demanded a sum of RS. 30 lakhs which was later on reduced to Rs. 29, 500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The wife of the deceased denied any aiding and abetting. The Presidency Magistrate who tried the case convicted him under section 19(1)(c) of 'the Act and sentenced him to one month 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30,000. The appeal preferred by the appellant was summarily dismissed on 20 2 1950. On 10 4 1950 the wife of appel late was acquitted, the evidence being insufficient to prove any abetment. The High Court rejected this contention on behalf of the appellants based on the language of section 19 (1) and this is the only point which required our consideration. Held:(i) An assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction. It was the landlord 's consent to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt of consideration that has been made an offen cientence. The section in question, it should be further noted does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. (ii) In the case of an assignment, the assignor contin ues to be liable to the landlord for the performance of his obligations under the tenancy and this liability is contrac tual, while the assignee becomes liable by reason of privity of estate. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. But in the case Of relinquishment, it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them. (iii) In fact, a surrender or relinquishment terminates the lessee 's rights and lets in the lessor. It could only be made in favour o the lessor through mutual agreement. The relin cation of possession must be to the lessor or one who holds his interest.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership concern and the workmen of the Tata Engineering Company Ltd. were members of the T minority Employees Union. The company function as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and did not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consisted of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of 665 employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306. These workmen were members Of the Tata Iron & Steel Company Ltd., and they served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. 170 The Union filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. It was urged that the Efficiency Bar as a feature of the wages scale should be removed, and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the union for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the company 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. On appeal, the Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appellant, and decided to modify the existing structure of scales with flat increases in each category. But it rejected the claim of the company for dearness allowances on the ground that there would be a consequent increase in the dearness allowance or house rent allowance. The Industrial Tribunal also noted that after the salaries of the employees had been fixed in the respective scales, senior employees would have to be given some more increments in the new scales according to their completed years of service. Rs. 150/ per month and Rs. 100/ respectively and Rs., 100/ above the existing wage scales. The award was challenged by the workmen before the Industrial Tribunal which held that the existing wages were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that the increase envisaged there related to an increase in dearness allowance, it was not possible for it to bear additional financial liability if the demand demands of Union were accept. It also observed that in view of the increased burden of Rs. 50/ per mensem, the company should have fixed the dearness allowances in communion with the cost of living index and should not be a fixed amount. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that having regard to the financial capacity of the Company, the Industrial Tribunals erred in making the wage scale retrospective and, in any event, in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January 1976. It is urged that having due regard to its financial capacity, the appellant Tribunal erred in passing the wage rates retrospective and in any case, in increasing the retrospectivity, back to 21st January, 1976. On behalf of workmen it was submitted that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs 150/ to each workman in the case of Draughtsmen and Rs 100/ and Rs, 100/ in the category of Draftsmen and of Rs,100/ to every employee in the other categories had been granted under the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957. It would be noted that the Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the Unions that a flat increased to the pay of each workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. This agreement was subsequently published in Bihar Gazette as a part of the award. In spite of the Award and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. / 10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages, and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents ' claim. It was urged that section 15 Of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The authority rejected the appellant 's contention and held that section 2 (vi) included wages prescribed under the Industrial Tribunal Act, and so it had rejected the appellants ' contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section15 of the , and dismissed the petition. Held: (i) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section2(vi)(a) cannot take in the wages prescribed in the award is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of the Industrial Disputes Act before it was amended. (ii) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection, the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1523, and V. B Godse, Manager, Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act, the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 of the . (iii) to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudica tion.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was part of his duties to disburse the wages to the workmen employed in the works and the procedure usually followed was that be drew the amount required from the treasury and paid the same to the em plo yees against their signatures or thumb impressions in the monthly acquittance roll. In the roll for April 1951, one Parma was mentioned as a khalasi (menial servant), and a sum of Rs. 51 shown as paid to him for his wages, the payment being vouched by thumb impression. The case of the prosecution was that there was an application by the Department for sanction to prosecute the appellant for an offence under section 409, and that the Chief Secretary, Home Department sent the communication, Exhibft PX, stating that he had been directed to convey sanction of the Government to his prosecution. In view of this, no question was raised before the trial Magistrate or the High Court that the prosecution had not established that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of Parma. The High Court held that the charge under section 477A required sanction as the official capacity was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime and that there having been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section409 and that sanction had not been obtained under section 198 (1) for his prosecution, that the evidence on record was insufficient to establish an offence either under section 465 or section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and that therefore sanction was required for a prosecution under that section. Held:(i) The charge under s. 477A requires sanction as "the official capacity is involved in very act alleged as amountingto a crime". (ii) The entrustment and/or dominion was 'in his capacity as a public servant '; third, that there could in this case be no disposal, lawful or otherwise save by an act done or purporting to be done in an official capacity. (iii)The entrustment and dominion here were in an Official capacity and it was equally evident that there can in this ease be no dispose, lawful, or otherwise, save by any act done by him while he is actually engaged in the performance of his official duties; but if they do, then sanction would be necessary; and (iv)the mere fact that the entrustment and /or dominion had been entered into in an officer capacity does not make it a matter relevant at the stage of sanction. Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli vs The King, [1948] L.R 75 I.A. 185, referred to.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. It filed its income for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore state and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs. 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. At the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax the following question was referred to the High Court of Travancore Cochin: " Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the loss of Rs 27,709 arising in Cochin State could be set off against the profit of Rs." The assessee contended that the first proviso to section 24(1)(i) did not apply to the head business business but only introduced an addendum that where the profits of the business arose in what is British India in the case of Travancore Act and the losses under the head 'business were sustained in an Indian State or in the latter case in any other Indian State, these losses could not by virtue of the proviso be deducted from profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. Held, that the object of section 24 was to allow a set off of profits arising under different heads and only in such cases could recourse be had to section 25(1). Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Incometax, Madras ([1950] S.C.R. 271), Ram Narain Sons Ltd. vs Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax (2) , distinguished.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. The Head Office of the Company is at Calcutta. It has branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The general practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices appears to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 though in certain cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees under which the age Of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the ageof 55 subject to their employees passing the medical examination at reaching the 58 of 55 subject, subject to certain employees passing in a medical examina tion on reaching that age of 60. In October 1959 an Agreement was entered between the company and its employee at Calcutta under which it was agreed that the age should be fixed at 60. The dispute was whether it should be fix at 58 or at 60, and it was found that in Bombay the age for workmen in all industries should be given at 60 years. The Tribunal held that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 60 60 years, but the Company may in its wisdom and with the express implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and that it was not correct to say that the error was established in fact. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Tribunal had rightly taken into account the fact that in the Bombay region at least there is a general agree ment that the. age of retirement should be raised at 60 and not at 55. The very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal has mentioned are wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend, and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter.

The first respondent was the Chairman of a company Law Board. The second respondent was appointed as an Inspector for investigating the affairs of the Barium Chemicals Ltd., appellant No. 1 before the Board. On June 4, 1965, the Company preferred a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the Punjab High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus or other appropriate writ directing the company Law Boards and Inspectors from giving effect to the order dated May 19, 1965 and also sought some other incidental reliefs. The order was challenged on the ground that the Chairman had acted mala fide because no honest opinion was formed on the matters which under the section give rise to the power but on irrelevant and extraneous material and further because the order was passed under the influence and malice of a Minister of Cabinet who was interested in another Company belonging to his sons and sought this means to oust a rival. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there were circumstances suggesting that as stated in the order of May 19 the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(b) of the ; (1) that the provisions of section 237 (b) were void as offending articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of ' the Constitution; (2) that there was ample material before the board on which it could and did form the opinion that there had been circumstances suggesting the need for action under section 237. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 of the , to order an investigation and delegated by it to the company law Board is administrative that it can be validly exercised by the Chairman by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central Govern ment under section 642(1) read with section 10E (5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the company, that there the opinion to be formed under section 236 is subjective and that if the grounds are disclosed by the Board the Court can examine them for considering whether they are relevant. The power conferred by section 239(b)(a) is merely administrative it is difficult to appreciate how the allocation of business of the Board relating to the exercise Of such power can be anything other than a matter of procedure. For sub section (6) of section 10 E, I am inclined to construe this rule making power liberally and the Central Govt has power to constitute the company 's board to control (1)(2) 342 The power is conferred on it but under the Companies Act, 1951, a Board of Company Law Administration consisting of a Chairman and a member has been set up.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to five years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . The High Court, on appeal by special leave, held that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, and therefore it was necessary always to start with the lesser presumption and draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime itself. In appeal by Special Leave, HELD : The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence, to connect an accused with the crime, it may be drawn. It is not necessary to state categorically in this case that the person with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. This presumption has been drawn and in our opinion rightly in this ease. [723 A] In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders and they had been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. It may be 723 impossible to think that these 20 persons were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who are the dacoits. The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. In two cases only the time gap is about 19 days. Even then, the time lag is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The petitioners were contending that in substance manufactured by them did not come within the amended Rules. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [225A B] 1.2 The provisions contained in neither Section 3 nor Section 5 nor Notification are hit either by any limitation limitation. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on the same. The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. (iv). [904 D E] Prakashchand Mehra vs Union of India, ; and Prakash Chand Mehta vs The Bank of workmen, ; followed.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel, filed an application before the High Court for grant of special leave to appeal against the decision of the High COurt. The appellants contended before this Court that the High Courts had not taken into account the relevant factors, particularly to the question of the migratory birds when they took the final decision to grant the lease and that there was no need to mention the needs and interests of the Zooo which were already well known and had also received consideration. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government of West Bengal acted perfectly bona fide in granting the lease of Begumbar land to a Taj Group for the construction of Five Star Hotel on the Begambari land as a policy decision to the hotel group to start a Five Star hotel on the Zoological Garden and that what had become statutorily vested in the Committee could not be divested by an execu tive fiat. [251C D] 1.2 In view of this policy, no resin would be auctioned by the State and there would be no question of sale of resin in the open market and in this situation, it would be totally irrelevant to import the concept of market price with reference to which the adequacy of the price charged by the state to the second respondents could be judged. [252E] 1:3 The Government had made available to the Court all the relevant documents so as to satisfy the court about the propriety of its action.

The assessee, Dr. R.S. Gupta had maintained an account in the books of Messrs. Tika Ram and Sons Pvt. On 1st January 1957, the account showed a credit of Rs. 1,50,000. The entries were made in the respective accounts. On that day, the assessee had addressed a letter to the Company stating that he had decided to gift away for love and affection various sums to the following persons: 125 Ved Prakash Gupta Rs.25,000 Om Prakash Gupta. Rs.50,00,000 Prem Prakash Gupta, Rs. 50,000 Suraj Prakash Gupta & Rs. 25,000 Ashok Gupta Rs .50, 000 Pravin Kumar Gupta Rs, Rs,50000 Om Parkash Gupta Rs.,25,00000 Suraj Parkash Gupta, RS.50000 Suraj Kumar Gupta,Rs.50.000 Om Prakesh Kumar Gupta. The assessee had also addressed a letters to the company stating that they had decided that gift away from his account to the extent of Rs 1, 50, 000 and credit the respective amounts in the names of the aforesaid per sons. It was further stated that copies of this letter were sent to one Om Prakash and Ved Prakash. There was no dispute that instructions of the assessee were car ried out by the Company and relevant debit and credit en tries were made In the respective account books. On the same day i.e. on 1st February, 1957, Om Parkash GUPTA wrote to the assessee, his father, thanking him for the gift of Rs 25,00 000 made in his favour and the gift was held to be valid. But there was no evidence that the interest which were credited in the accounts of the minor donees was allowable as a deduc tion in the hands of the asses see firm. The Tribunal held that the sum of Rs 67,560/12 was rightly included in the assessee 's net wealth by the Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. It also held that there was not valid gifts. In reference under section 27(1) of the Act, the High Court answered the first question in the negative and so far as the second question is concerned, it declined to answer as it did not arise in view of the answer given to the first ques tions and the questions Nos. In case of entries in the book of account by credit and debit, the sums should be available on the date of gift in the account of the firm whose accounts are said to be credited or debited. In the case of banking companies or other firms and companies who have overdraft facilities, even if the sums are not in credit of the donor and are not with such companies or firms, gifts might be possible by adjustment of the book entries. But in the cases of non banking companies and firms, if these companies or firm do not have overdraft facility, it is not possible to make valid gift if sums or funds are not available. It is possible in certain circumstances for a donor to make a valid gift by instructing a firm or a company or a H.U.F. in which the donor has an account to give effect to the gift by debiting his account and crediting the account in his name of the donee. The circumstances must be such as to make it clear that there were sufficient funds at the disposal of the doner by reason of which he could make the gift, by such book entries, and the firm in which he may have account may or may not have sufficient cash balance but it must have sufficient provision for overdraft with the bank on the basis it could honour in structions given by the assessee. This position of law has been referred to and reiterated by the Bench decision of the Delhi High Court in the case Of Commissioner of Gift Tax, West Bengal 111 vs Ashok Glass Works, , wherein it was held that gifts were valid though not sufficient cash with firm avail able but proper book entries were mad e. The High Court also took divergent views.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to Government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio Additional law secretary to the government in law Department, member administrative tribunal and the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, in all 15 in number. All these officers are the members of the service of the State and they were before 1962 presiding over district courts or courts subordinate to them and as such were under the control of the High Court. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of the administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The Government by its letter of April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to adhere to the principle of three years service in an appointment at a particular station against a special post. But when it came to the question of implementing that policy, the government was reluctant. Every time the High court requested the Government to release the three officers mentioned above for being posted as district and Session judges or addl. district and session judges as the case may be, the Government turned down those requests on one ground or the other. But at that stage the High 's Court felt helpless as it was under the impression that under law the Governor was the sole authority to effect the necessary transfers. The government implemented the orders in question on March 6, 1967 and intimated that the Government had no objections to adhere with the principle. The order of the high court is set aside.

Section 15 of the 1913 Act as it originally stood, underwent substantial changes in 1960 and as a result thereof, a host of writ petitions 122 were filed in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of section 15 on the ground that it infringed Articles 14 and 15 of tho Constitution. The petition ers contended that he fell within the expression other co sharers ' in cl. (Fourthly) of section15(1)(b) and was, therefore, entitled to claim the right of pre emption under clause 'fourthly ' of section fifteen(1) (b). A similar question came up before this Court in Balwant Ram vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , wherein a two judge Bench of this Court negatived the contention in the follow ing words: "In order to understand the meaning of the words 'other co sharer ' in clause 'Fourthly ' occurring in section 15(1), it is clear that the legislature desired to confer the right on specified family members of the vendor or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section '15(i)(b). Since this Court found certain intrinsic contradictions in the list of relatives covered by the first three cls, it saw no justification for the classification contained in the said provision conferring a right based on consanguinity and, therefore struck down those clauses. The appellant contended that the interpretation placed by the two judge bench on the expression 'other Co sharers" in section15 (1)(a) of the Act was to deny the right conferred on co shar er i.e. father 's broth er 's son of the vendors and the tenants constitut ed a distinct class by themselves, the right to pre empt was upheld as reasonable and in public interest. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The purport of the Court 's decision in Attam Prakash 's case was to denying the right Of pre emation to those relative or relatives of the ly vendor or ly vendors who are specified in tho erstwhile first 3 clauses of Section 15(i) (a), even if they happen to be co sharors.

The workmen of the appellant company, who were workers in the respondent 's industry, claimed that they were entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of illness for which sickness benefit was last paid. The workmen also felt aggrieved because by virtue of the first proviso to section 49 of the , they were not entitled to sickness benefit under the scheme of the Act. The company resisted both the cases on the ground that the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of tile Act were already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Allowing the appeals by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribunal. [83C] 2.1 In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the grounds of sickness. [86D] 2:2 The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in its view that the workmen are entitled to 7 days sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. [87E F] 3.1 The benefit of sick leave has been allowed to the workmen of those companies. It would thus appear that the appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question were illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [888A] 3:3 The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit of 7 days Sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It will thus appear from the record that even though the Act was applicable to the workers of the Precision Bearings India Ltd., Baroda, Hindustan Brown Bovari Ltd., and M.S. University Press, Baroda, the benefit could not b.e said to be adequate for it works out to about half the average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the 1st two days ' of sickness excepting in the ease of a period of sickness certified at an intervals of not less than 15 day, the period of illness would be very much beyond the paying capacity of the industry. [898B C] 4:4 The Tribunal had examined this question also and gave adequate reasons to allow the benefit to the sick leave. [90C] 5. In the instant case, the appellants had not been unable to show any reason to disagree with the view which it has taken. As has been stated, the Act came into force in the region concerned on December 14. 1969, till then it was the practice in the glass industries to grant sick leave without wages for periods varying from 6 to 10 days. [91G] 6:5 The Tribunal could not therefore be said that to have erred in restoring the benefit which the workmen were re ceiving under the award of 1958, for it was taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the .

The appellant was detained under the , by an order of detention passed against him on the 8th June, 1955, and was served with a copy of the grounds of detention. The validity of the order was challenged on the following grounds: (1) that there was a sudden search by the police on the 24th August, 1954 at the appellant 's place for alleged possession of illicit liquor; (2) that the detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan National Movement and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos. Held, that the order of the detention was mala fide. The grounds furnished in this case were open to challenge of vagueness, the further question which arose is whether the validity of an order can be sustained by reason of the claim, in public interest, of non disclosure of facts made by the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay by means of his affidavit filed in the High Court. The State itself could not support the said highhandedness. The power not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of the detenue for being afforded a reasonable opportunity to make a representation to the Board. In the present case there was no merit in this contention.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He was charged with having committed acts which amounted to gross misconduct under section 45 of the . The respondent contended that he did not assist Kumari Prakash to go away from his parents ' house. At the hearing of the petition, the only point which was urged was the validity of r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. Held, that r.14 of the Defence Rules, 1955, is not ultra vires the . It was argued by the respondent that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. The power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words 'subject to . the provisions .of this Act ', it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. For removal from service under section19 of the read with r. 13 of the Rules, the Central Govern ment may remove a "person from the serv ice". Rule 14 is not therefore ultra vires.

The appellant was a Panchayat under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946 (C.P.) and by virtue of this Act the appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat. On July 14, 1961, the Bombay Village Panchayat passed resolution No. 2 with a view to levy octroi duty. The resolution further provided that the meeting considered the question of imposition of octroi duty and the number and location of octroi Nakas within the limits of the jurisdiction of the Panchayat under r. 21. The appellant filed an appeal before the Standing Committee on October 22, 1963. While the appeal was pending, the Tehsildar Ramtek on January 14, 1964 approved the octroi limits and the numbers and location thereof were fixed by the Collector. On March 17, 1963, a resolution No, 5 was passed which provided that in case of failure to comply with the provisions of the Act, the appellant would be liable to pay octroi duty at the rate of Rs. 1/ per day. The company thereupon filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of octroi tax. The High Court held that the octroi duty was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed to fix the octroi limit in accordance with law and therefore, the imposition of the octroi from April 1, 1963 was regularised. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was intra vires (2) that the Standing committee had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal on merits as the appeal to the Panchayat Samiti was barred by limitation because r. 3(b) did not require the Panchayat to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the rules. HELD: (i) The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea was crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. [218 B] (ii) The fixing of octroi limits with the approval of the Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy. of octroi duties. The procedure prescribed in rr. 3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi tax can start being levied, r.21 must be complied with. [217 C D] (iii) The fixation of the rate at which it was to be levied and the rate from which it is to be imposed and the rates at which the same was to he levied. [216 E F] (iv) The procedure for levying taxes or fees is not confined to octroi duty only. Rule 7 which deals with tax on buildings and lands also prescribes that the Panchayat shall follow the procedure prescribed therein in rr 3 and4 before levying a tax on building and lands. Similarly, rs. 33 which deals With tax on pilgrims provides that the procedure laid down in rr,3 and 4 shall be followed. [214 E] (v) The scheme of the fees Rules is first to prescribe general rules and then to deal with various taxes mentioned in the other parts of the Rules. Viewed in this background it seems to us that r .3(b), does not require that the panchayat to notify the public cannot only the proposals about the levy proposed by it, but also that the rules relate to that taxation which must include the action already taken under that Act and rules.

C. vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co. Ltd., [1955] 2 S.C.R. 869, referred to. The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he 's activities were prejudicial to maintenance of public order. The grounds of detention stated as follows: 1. On 24.12.1985 between 10 and 10.30 A.M., the subject alongwith Ramashish Bangali, Gulam, Rambriksha armed with Rifle, gun etc came in Car No. BHG 9372 on Katras Coal Dump and started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish his criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers, customers and passers by of the area. The normal tempo of life was completely disturbed. The people started running helter and skelter for their lives. Shopkeepers put down their shutters. Doors and windows were closed. The vehicular traffic came to halt. This refers to Katras P.S. Case No. 331/85 dated 24.10.85 u/s 147, 341/353/307 I.P.C. In this case, subject and his associates tried to set free the trucks and driver from the police custody by force and when he failed in his attempt he threatened the police officer and abused the police officers and policemen to do away with their lives, C.S No. 5/83 had already been submitted in this case. Jogta P. S. Case NO. 22/84 dated 11.3.1984 u/ss 147, 148, 307/149/324 I. P.C., Arms Act. In the said case, the petitioner/appellant was arrested on 2nd January, 1986 and he was taken into custody. The order of detention though dated 2nd February, 1986 was served on or about 11th January,1986. It is the case of the detenu that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. The service of order of deten tion on the petitioner while he was in jail was futile and useless since such an order had no application under section 2(2). Nor does it appear that before the Service there was consideration of this aspect properly. [910G] (b) The order is set aside. The writ petition and the appeal are allowed to the extent indicated above. [ 909A B] (c) In the instant case, when the actual order of Detention was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in Jail.

Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down sec. 28 of Act on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an unguided, uncanalised discretion upon the administrator with the results that the licence is at mercy of the Administrator and is help less against the arbitrary exercise of the power by the Administrator when he chooses to negative the request. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that sec.28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The objective, the policy and the Scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. In fact, sec. 5(1) requires that the Administrator should have regard to the anticipated demand ' as estimated by him for the ornaments in that region but the expression 'anticipated demand ' was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression (1)AIR 1971 Patna 240; (2)14 Guj. L.R. 112. 106.suitability of the applicant ' in cl. (e) and 'public interest ' in el. (g) A did not provide any objective standard or norm and because such indefinite, uncertain and vague expressions or concepts had been used in some of the clauses under secs. 27(6) this Court struck aside sec. 27 on the grounds of excessive delegated power. [955E F] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona II Division while declaring unamended sec.27(6), as it stood prior to its amendment by the Amending Act No. 26 of 1969, constitutionally invalid on the view that it conferred a very wide and vague power upon Administrator to grant or renew a license to a dealer the unamended secs 27(1). [956G H] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthria vs Union of lndia, ; , referred to.

The trial Judge found that the grant of the Inam was a personal Inam and that it was not a grant in favour Of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) Article 134 B applied to all cases where it is shown that the immovable property was comprised in the endowment and that there was no distinction between the office and the property of the endowment. The character of the representations made by the previous manager in regard to his relation with the property which is the subject matter of transfer, is irrelevant for the purpose of article 134 B.
